column1: 🗳  VOTE MAXIMIZER — VOTER POWER CALCULATOR  |  2026 ELECTION CYCLE
Hybrid sigma methodology  |  Metamargin=0.0 (neutral)  |  Turnout scaling: ÷turnout^0.3  |  🟢 green margin = real poll  |  🟡 amber margin = Cook proxy
📖  METHODOLOGY — HOW THE HYBRID SIGMA APPROACH WORKS

column4:
Voter Power (unnormalized) = t-PDF( (margin − metamargin) / σ_eff,  df ) × (σ_eff / σ_Senate) ÷ turnout^0.3 × 1,000,000

voter_power (0–100) = 100 × VP_raw ÷ max(VP_raw within race type)

The three key adjustable parameters: margin (from polls or Cook rating), σ_eff (race-type specific), metamargin (national environment).

σ_polling = 3.0 pts — how far polls might be off on Election Day (Sam Wang's estimate from 2024 methodology).
σ_historical = race-type swing based on EIL historical data (Senate 7.97, Governor 11.72, Ballot 16.90, etc.).

These measure different things. Polling error tells you how uncertain the current estimate is. Historical swing tells you how much that race TYPE tends to move over time. Both matter: a ballot measure with σ_hist=16.9 is inherently more volatile than a Senate race with σ_hist=7.97, so its VP should be somewhat higher even at the same poll margin.

σ_eff = σ_polling + (σ_historical − σ_polling) × 0.25

Effective sigmas used:
  • US Senate:         4.24 pts  (reference; ratio = 1.00×)
  • US House:          4.00 pts  (matches 2024 VM formula exactly)
  • Governor:          5.18 pts  (ratio = 1.22×)
  • AG / Sec of State: 5.00 pts  (ratio = 1.18×)
  • State Legislature: 3.96 pts  (ratio = 0.93× — lower because districts are more entrenched)
  • Ballot Initiatives: 6.47 pts  (ratio = 1.53× — highest, most volatile)

A wider σ_eff flattens the PDF peak, which would naively reduce VP for volatile race types. To correct for this, each race's VP is multiplied by (σ_eff / σ_Senate). This means: at the same poll margin, a ballot initiative gets 1.53× the VP of an equivalent Senate race, a Governor race gets 1.22×, and so on. The effect grows for non-tossup races: at lean-D (+4 pts), a ballot measure retains 72% of its tossup VP, while a Senate race retains only 53% — correctly reflecting that ballot measures can swing more.

🟢 GREEN "poll" = real polling average used, sourced from Emerson/PPP/ASR/Sabato Jan–Mar 2026.
🟡 AMBER "cook" = Cook Political Report rating proxy (toss-up=0, lean=±4, likely=±9, solid=±18).

As actual polls become available, replace the Cook proxy with real margins in the "Poll Margins" column of each dataset tab. VP scores will recalibrate automatically. Priority: populate margins for all toss-up and lean races first.

Statewide races: divide by turnout^0.3 (gentle size correction). A Maine tossup scores ~94% of Alaska's tossup because Maine's electorate is larger (800k vs 360k). Large competitive states like Georgia (5M) and NC (5.5M) still score in the top 10 for Senate. Solid-state small races score 3–7 — very low but not exactly zero, which is mathematically correct (even a solid race has a non-zero but tiny chance of flipping under extreme conditions).
House: no turnout scaling — all districts are equal population by law.

1. Replace Cook proxies with real poll averages as they become available (esp. toss-up and lean races).
2. Calibrate the metamargin from generic ballot data (currently 0.0 = neutral environment).
3. Update the 2026 turnout estimate if early-cycle data suggests a departure from 2020 patterns.
